theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: An office supplies distributor in Kingston sells to hotels, schools and law firms rather than to members of the public. How is this kind of trade usually described?
options: Business-to-consumer (B2C) trade
Business-to-business (B2B) trade
Retail trade with the general public
Direct export trade to overseas buyers

questions.stem: Compared with selling to members of the public, which feature is most typical of selling to business customers?
options: Most purchases are made on impulse by one person
Prices are fixed by the seller and are seldom discussed
Orders are small and are paid for in cash
Several people in the buying firm shape the decision

questions.stem: Before a first meeting with the purchasing manager of a large Ocho Rios hotel, what should the account manager find out first?
options: The hotel's needs, current suppliers and buying process
The hotel's staff turnover over the last five years
The personal interests of the hotel's general manager
The full price list of every rival supplier in the parish

questions.stem: At a manufacturing firm, the production supervisor tests a new lubricant and tells the buyer whether it works well. In the decision-making unit (the group that shapes a purchase), what role is the supervisor playing?
options: Gatekeeper
Decider
Influencer
Payer

questions.stem: A sales executive's emails to a hospital's finance director never get past the director's personal assistant. In the decision-making unit, what role is the assistant playing?
options: Gatekeeper
User
Initiator
Buyer

questions.stem: A May Pen agricultural supplier has 300 business accounts. Its sales records show that about 60 of them provide most of its gross profit. Which approach makes best use of this?
options: Serve every account in exactly the same way to be fair to all
Close the 240 smaller accounts to save staff time
Raise prices for the 60 accounts that buy the most
Give the top 60 accounts closer service and planned contact

questions.stem: What does the Pareto principle (the 80/20 rule) suggest about a firm's business customers?
options: About 80% of customers are usually unhappy with service
A small share of customers often brings most of the sales
About 20% of all invoices from customers are usually paid late
Most new customers leave within the first 20 weeks

questions.stem: Which customer is most likely to be treated as a key account by a Montego Bay laundry service?
options: A guest house that sends linen once a month
A walk-in customer who pays in cash for each load every week
A resort group that makes up a large share of income
A new café that has asked for a price list

questions.stem: Shanice Brown has just been made key account manager for a supermarket chain. What is the main purpose of the account plan she should write?
options: To set objectives and actions to grow the account
To record the chain's complaints over the past year
To list the products the chain bought last month
To show her own sales targets to the chain's buyers

questions.stem: A firm's sales staff each keep customer details in their own notebooks and phones. What is the main business benefit of moving to a shared customer relationship management (CRM) system?
options: Staff no longer need to speak to customers by phone
The firm no longer needs a data protection policy
Every business customer will be offered the same discount
Contact history stays with the firm if a person leaves

questions.stem: Six months after a CRM system went live, the sales manager finds that half the team still record nothing in it. What should she do first?
options: Replace it with a different CRM system from another supplier
Find out why, then fix the causes with training and rules
Issue written warnings to everyone not using it
Let staff choose whether they use it or not

questions.stem: Which CRM report would best help a manager spot business customers who may be about to leave?
options: Accounts whose orders have dropped sharply in three months
Accounts that were opened during the last month of the year
Accounts with the longest company names on file
Accounts that are handled by the newest staff

questions.stem: A Spanish Town security company and its client write down the response time, reporting and standards the client can expect. What is this document usually called?
options: A purchase order
A delivery note
A service level agreement
A letter of credit

questions.stem: Why should a service level agreement with a business customer state how performance will be measured?
options: So that the customer cannot complain at any time
So that the price can be raised at any point during the contract
So that the supplier's staff can work fewer hours
So that both sides judge the service in the same way

questions.stem: At the start of the year a courier firm had 200 business accounts. It lost 30 of them during the year and won 50 new ones. What was its customer retention rate for the year?
Why do many firms find it worth spending effort to keep existing business customers?
options: Winning new customers usually costs more than keeping current ones
Existing customers never ask for lower prices or better terms of trade
Existing customers are not covered by data protection law
New customers always pay their invoices later than old ones

questions.stem: A business client of a Portmore printing firm places 8 orders a year at an average of J$150,000 each. The firm earns a gross margin of 25% and expects to keep the client for 4 years. What is the client's expected lifetime gross profit?
An account brings in sales of J$5,000,000 a year. The goods cost J$3,500,000 and the cost to serve the account (delivery, visits, credit and support) is J$1,800,000. What does this show?
options: The account makes a profit of J$1,500,000
The account makes a profit of J$300,000
The account makes a loss of J$300,000
The account breaks even exactly

questions.stem: A review shows that a large business customer is served at a loss because of many small rush deliveries. What is the best first step?
options: Stop supplying the customer from next week
Discuss ordering patterns and terms with the customer
Add a hidden charge to each of the customer's invoices
Keep serving the customer as before and say nothing

questions.stem: In a survey of business clients, 60% are promoters and 15% are detractors. What is the net promoter score (NPS)?
A firm surveys its business customers each year, but nothing changes afterwards. What is the most likely effect over time?
options: Customers will rate the firm more highly each year
Staff will learn more from each survey than before
Fewer customers will bother to give feedback
The survey results will become more accurate

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a regular account review meeting with a key business customer?
options: To check results against the plan and agree next steps
To announce the supplier's new prices for the year
To collect payment for any of the client's invoices that are overdue
To introduce the supplier's newest members of staff

questions.stem: During an account review, a client says a rival is offering the same service for 10% less. What should the account manager do first?
options: Match the rival's price at once to keep the account
Tell the client the rival's service is poor

Ask questions to understand what is being compared

questions.stem: A stationery supplier that already sells paper to a law firm also offers it printer servicing. What is this called?
options: Upselling
Cross-selling
Discounting
Prospecting

questions.stem: Which is the soundest reason to offer a business customer a larger or better product?
options: It will meet a need the customer has shown
The supplier has too much of it in stock
It carries the highest commission for staff
The customer has never asked about it before

questions.stem: A hotel group's procurement manager emails an angry complaint about a late delivery that delayed a conference. What should the account manager do first?
options: Send the standard apology letter used for all customers
Wait until the warehouse report is ready before replying to the email
Reply promptly, acknowledge the problem and find out its impact
Offer a large discount before learning the facts

questions.stem: After solving a serious complaint from a business customer, what step most helps prevent the same problem with other accounts?
options: Thank the staff member who dealt with the customer
Find the root cause and change the process
Send the customer a small gift as goodwill

questions.stem: Which statement about complaints from business customers is most accurate?
options: A complaint means the account is already lost to a rival firm
Only written complaints need to be recorded
Complaints should be handled by the newest staff
A complaint handled well can strengthen the relationship

questions.stem: A new business customer asks for 60-day credit on a large first order. What should the supplier do before agreeing?
options: Check the customer's credit standing and set a limit
Agree at once to make sure the large first order is won
Refuse all credit to every new customer
Ask the sales staff to guess what is safe

questions.stem: A loyal client is often slow to pay, but buys a lot. Which approach best protects both the relationship and the firm's cash?
options: Stop all deliveries without telling the client why
Ignore the late payments because the client buys a lot
Pass the debt to a collection agency straight away
Agree clear terms and follow up early and politely

questions.stem: A hotel group asks for a 15% discount when it renews a two-year supply contract. Which response is most likely to protect value for both sides?
options: Agree to the full 15% because the contract is so large and valuable
Refuse any change and repeat the current price
Trade a smaller discount for a longer term or larger volume
Ask the hotel group to name a lower figure

questions.stem: Before negotiating a contract renewal, an account manager works out the lowest terms she can accept and her best option if no deal is reached. Why is this useful?
options: It means the customer will accept her first offer
It lets her know when to stop and walk away
It removes the need to plan the meeting
It allows her to hide the price from the customer

questions.stem: A key client has asked to be told at once about any delay in its orders. A shipment will be two days late. What should the account manager do?
options: Call the client now, explain and give a new date
Wait to see whether the shipment arrives on time
Ask the warehouse staff to tell the client later
Send the goods without mentioning the delay

questions.stem: Which plan for keeping in touch with a large business customer is most suitable?
options: Contact only when an invoice is due for payment
Daily phone calls to the most senior manager at the customer's firm
Contact only when the customer raises a problem
An agreed mix of reviews, updates and contacts at each level

questions.stem: Why do many firms link several of their staff with different staff at a key client, not just one account manager with one buyer?
options: So that each person has less work to do
So that no one person is responsible for the account
So the relationship does not depend on one contact
So the client can be given more discounts

questions.stem: An experienced account manager is leaving the firm next month. What should her manager do to protect her key accounts?
options: Plan a handover with joint visits and full CRM notes
Wait until she has gone, then assign the accounts
Ask the clients to call the main office if needed
Give the accounts to the newest member of staff

questions.stem: A sales manager wants her account managers to focus on keeping and growing accounts, not only on new sales. Which change best supports this?
options: Pay a bonus only for each brand-new account won
Include retention and account growth in their targets
Cut the number of visits each manager may make
Let each manager set their own targets alone

questions.stem: A client's buyer hints that a personal gift would help the supplier win a contract. What should the account manager do?
options: Give a small gift, as is common in business
Ask a colleague to arrange the gift instead
Raise the contract price to cover the cost of the gift
Decline, record it and report it under company policy

questions.stem: An account manager learns a client's confidential expansion plans during a meeting. A rival of the client is also a customer. What should she do?
options: Share the plans with the rival to help both sides
Mention the plans to the rival in general terms
Keep the information confidential within the firm
Post a hint about the plans on social media

questions.stem: A firm stores the names, phone numbers and emails of contacts at its business clients. Which practice is in line with the data protection law?
options: Sell the contact list to another firm for a fee
Keep the data secure and use it only for agreed purposes
Keep the data for ever in case it is needed later
Share the list with any staff member who asks for it

questions.stem: A sales executive's laptop holding client records is stolen from his car. What should happen first?
options: Report it at once under the firm's data breach procedure
Buy a new laptop and reload the records from a backup
Wait to see whether the laptop is returned within a week
Tell the clients to change their passwords at once

questions.stem: Which measure best shows how well a firm is managing its existing business customers?
options: The number of sales calls made each week
The number of brochures printed in the year
The cost of the firm's new delivery van

questions.stem: A firm's business customer satisfaction scores rose, but several large accounts still left. What is the best conclusion?
options: Satisfaction surveys should be stopped for good
The accounts that left were never profitable
The survey may not reach the people who make decisions
The firm's prices must be far too low

questions.stem: After several talks, a business customer remains unprofitable and refuses any change in terms. What is the most professional way to end supply?
options: Give notice under the contract, explain and help with handover
Stop answering the customer's calls and emails until it goes away
Raise the price without notice so it leaves
Send its next orders late until it gives up

questions.stem: A firm loses three key accounts in one year. Which action should its manager take first?
options: Cut prices for all remaining customers
Hire more sales staff to replace the lost sales as quickly as possible
Change the firm's logo and advertising

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Give the three-letter abbreviation for trade between one business and another.
What do the letters CRM stand for?
Give the three-letter abbreviation for a written agreement that sets out the standard of service a customer can expect.
What two-word term is used for a business customer so important that it gets its own plan and manager?
What is the one-word name for the person in a buying firm who controls the flow of information and access to the decision-makers?
What three-letter abbreviation is used for the group of people in a firm who together shape a buying decision?
By what name is the 80/20 rule also known?
What one-word term describes the rate at which customers stop buying from a firm over a period?
A firm started the year with 400 business accounts. It lost 60 and gained 80. What was its retention rate, as a percentage?
Give the three-letter abbreviation for the customer loyalty measure found by taking the percentage of detractors away from the percentage of promoters.
In a client survey, 52% are promoters, 30% are passives and 18% are detractors. What is the net promoter score?
What term describes persuading a customer to buy a more costly or higher-grade version of what they already buy?
Give the three-letter abbreviation for the total profit a firm expects to earn from a customer over the whole relationship.
A client buys J$2,400,000 of goods a year. The goods cost J$1,680,000 and the cost to serve the client is J$540,000. What is the account's annual profit in J$?
Name the type of software system used to record every contact, order and note about a firm's customers in one place.

essays.stem: A Kingston catering supplier has just won a two-year contract to supply a large hotel group on the north coast. Plan how the supplier should manage this as a key account in the first year.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first name one key account manager and a deputy, and link our people to theirs at each level: the account manager with the purchasing manager, our operations lead with the hotels' chefs, and our finance officer with their accounts team. I would then write an account plan. It would profile the hotel group, map who decides, who uses and who influences purchases, set objectives such as 98% on-time delivery and growth into two more product lines, and list the actions, owners and dates. The service level agreement would set order cut-off times, delivery windows and how complaints are handled. Every contact and order would be recorded in the CRM system. I would hold a short monthly check with the purchasing manager and a quarterly review with senior staff, comparing results with the plan. I would also track the account's profit, including the cost to serve, so growth does not come at a loss. At the end of the year I would ask for formal feedback and update the plan before renewal talks.
markingPoints: Names an account manager and links staff at several levels of both firms
Writes an account plan with a customer profile, decision-makers, objectives and actions
Uses a service level agreement and a CRM system to set and record the service
Sets a review routine (monthly and quarterly) against the plan
Tracks account profitability and gathers feedback before renewal

essays.stem: A courier firm finds that its third-largest business client brings in J$6,000,000 a year in sales, but delivery costs J$4,200,000 and other costs to serve the client come to J$2,100,000. Evaluate the options open to the firm and recommend what it should do.
essays.modelAnswer: The figures show sales of J$6,000,000 against total costs of J$6,300,000 (J$4,200,000 plus J$2,100,000), so the client loses the firm J$300,000 a year. The options are to keep things as they are, to drop the client, or to change the way the account is served or priced. Keeping things as they are is not sustainable, because the loss grows with every extra delivery. Dropping the client stops the loss but also removes J$6,000,000 of sales, may leave drivers and vans idle, and could harm the firm's name with other clients if done badly. The best first choice is to change the account. I would study which costs drive the loss, for example rush jobs or many small parcels to remote parishes. I would then meet the client, show the facts openly and propose changes: set collection times, a minimum parcel charge, or a surcharge for same-day service. If the client accepts, the account can become profitable. If it refuses after fair talks, I would give notice under the contract and end supply politely.
markingPoints: Works out correctly that the account makes a loss of J$300,000
Weighs keeping the account unchanged and explains why it is not sustainable
Weighs dropping the client, including lost sales, idle capacity and reputation
Recommends finding the cost drivers and renegotiating service or price with the client
Gives a fall-back of ending supply fairly under the contract if talks fail

essays.stem: A Mandeville building supplies firm plans to bring in a customer relationship management (CRM) system for its trade customers. Evaluate the benefits and the risks, and recommend how to introduce it.
essays.modelAnswer: A CRM system would hold every trade customer's contacts, orders, quotes, complaints and credit notes in one place. The benefits are that any staff member can see the full history, the firm keeps knowledge when staff leave, managers can spot accounts whose orders are falling, and follow-ups are less likely to be missed. The data also helps the firm segment customers and plan visits. The risks are cost, time lost while staff learn the system, poor data if staff do not enter information, and the danger of a data breach, since the system holds personal details covered by the data protection law. I would recommend a planned introduction. First agree what the firm needs the system to do and choose one that fits the budget. Clean the existing customer data before loading it. Train staff, with a champion in each team, and start with a short pilot. Set simple rules on what must be recorded and check use weekly. Control access with passwords and roles, and review the results after six months.
markingPoints: Explains benefits: shared history, kept knowledge, spotting falling accounts, follow-up
Explains risks: cost, learning time, poor data entry, data protection
Recommends defining needs, cleaning data and piloting before full use
Includes training, champions and clear rules on recording
Includes access control and a review of results

essays.stem: A school board in St Ann complains that the furniture your firm delivered for a new block is the wrong size and the term starts in ten days. Describe how you would handle the complaint and keep the account.
essays.modelAnswer: I would call the board's contact the same day, apologise for the trouble and listen carefully to find out exactly what is wrong, how many items are affected and what the deadline means for the school. I would confirm the details in writing so we both have the same record. I would then check the order, the delivery note and the specification to find out where the mistake happened, without blaming anyone in front of the client. Next I would offer a clear solution with a date: for example, collecting the wrong items and delivering the right ones within seven days, with temporary furniture if needed so the term can start. I would give the client one named contact and update them at agreed times until the job is complete. Afterwards I would check that the client is satisfied, record the complaint and outcome in the CRM system, and find the root cause, such as an unclear order form, so it is fixed for every customer. A quick, honest response can leave the client trusting us more than before.
markingPoints: Responds the same day, apologises and listens to understand the impact
Confirms the facts in writing and checks the records to find the error
Offers a clear solution with dates that meets the deadline
Keeps one named contact and gives regular updates until complete
Records the complaint, finds the root cause and fixes the process

essays.stem: A Kingston wholesale distributor treats all 500 of its business customers the same way. Justify a change to managing them in groups based on their value and needs, and describe how the groups could be served.
essays.modelAnswer: Treating every customer the same wastes effort, because customers differ greatly in what they buy, what they need and what they earn for the firm. Sales records will probably show that a small share of customers brings most of the gross profit, as the Pareto principle suggests. I would rank the customers by annual gross profit and growth potential, then group them. The top group, perhaps 30 accounts, would become key accounts, each with a named manager, an account plan, regular reviews and agreed service levels. A middle group would get planned visits or calls each quarter and offers matched to their buying pattern. Small customers would be served efficiently through phone, email and an online order form, with clear standard terms. I would also look at needs, not only value: for example, hotels and schools may need different delivery times. The change lets the firm put its best people where the returns are highest, keeps smaller accounts well served at lower cost, and gives managers clear targets for each group.
markingPoints: Explains why one approach for all wastes effort, using value differences or the Pareto principle
Describes ranking customers by profit and potential to form groups
Describes the service for key accounts (manager, plan, reviews, service levels)
Describes lower-cost service for middle and small customers
Considers needs as well as value, and states the benefits of the change

essays.stem: A hotel group that buys J$40,000,000 of cleaning products a year from your firm asks for a 12% price cut at renewal. Plan how you would prepare for and conduct the negotiation.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by preparing the facts: the account's sales, gross margin and cost to serve, so I know what a 12% cut would do to profit. I would set my aims and limits: my ideal outcome, the lowest terms I could accept, and my best alternative if no deal is reached. I would also try to understand the hotel group's position: why it wants a cut, what rivals may have offered, and what else it values, such as reliable delivery, staff training or credit terms. I would get approval from my manager for the range I can offer. In the meeting I would listen first and ask questions to find the real concern. Rather than just cutting price, I would trade: a smaller discount in return for a longer contract, larger orders, fewer deliveries or a wider range of products. I would keep the tone friendly and focus on long-term value for both sides. Finally I would summarise what was agreed, confirm it in writing and update the contract and CRM record.
markingPoints: Prepares account figures and the effect of the cut on profit
Sets an ideal outcome, a walk-away point and a best alternative
Researches the customer's reasons and what else it values
Trades concessions (term, volume, service) rather than only cutting price
Summarises and confirms the agreement in writing

essays.stem: Design a programme for gathering and using feedback from the business customers of a Montego Bay office equipment servicing firm. Justify each part.
essays.modelAnswer: I would use several methods, because each shows something different. After each service call, a short two-question survey by text or email would measure satisfaction while the visit is fresh. Once a year I would run a fuller survey, including the net promoter question, sent to the decision-makers and the users at each client, because they often see the service differently. For key accounts I would hold a review meeting each quarter to discuss results face to face, which gives deeper and more honest feedback. I would also record every complaint and compliment in the CRM system, as these are feedback too. All results would be analysed by account and by type of problem, and shared with the service team each month. Most important, the firm must act on what it hears and tell customers what has changed, for example faster parts supply. This shows customers that their views matter and keeps them willing to respond. I would review the programme each year and keep personal data secure under the data protection law.
markingPoints: Uses a short survey after each service visit, justified by timeliness
Uses an annual survey reaching both decision-makers and users
Uses review meetings with key accounts and records complaints and compliments
Analyses results and shares them with staff
Acts on feedback and reports back to customers, with data kept secure

essays.stem: Discuss the ethical issues an account manager may face when managing large business customers, and recommend how a firm should guide its staff.
essays.modelAnswer: Account managers build close ties with customers, which brings ethical risks. Clients' buyers may offer or ask for gifts, meals or favours that could look like bribes. Staff may learn confidential information, such as a client's plans or prices, and be tempted to use it with other customers. There may be pressure to promise delivery dates or results the firm cannot meet, or to hide a problem to protect a sale. Conflicts of interest can arise if a staff member has a personal link with a client. Personal data about client contacts must also be protected under the data protection law. I would recommend that the firm writes a clear code of conduct covering gifts and hospitality, with a value limit and a gifts register, confidentiality, honest selling and conflicts of interest. Staff should be trained in it, with real cases to discuss. Targets and bonuses should not reward selling at any cost. There should be a safe way to report concerns, and managers should set an example and act firmly when the code is broken.
markingPoints: Identifies gifts, favours and bribery risks
Identifies confidentiality and misuse of client information
Identifies honest selling, conflicts of interest or data protection issues
Recommends a written code with a gifts register and training
Recommends fair targets, safe reporting and managers setting an example

essays.stem: A Portmore security firm has lost 20% of its business clients in a year. Plan an investigation into why, and recommend ways to improve retention.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by listing the clients who left, with their size, length of contract, service history and the date they left, from the CRM system and the accounts records. I would then contact as many as possible, ideally through a manager who did not serve them, and ask politely why they left and what would have kept them. I would also talk to the guards and supervisors who served those sites, and compare complaint records and response times for lost clients with those for clients who stayed. I would look for patterns: for example, losses after a price rise, in one parish, or under one supervisor. Possible improvements, depending on the findings, are a named account manager for larger clients, regular review meetings, faster response to complaints, clear service level agreements, better training for guards, and an early warning report in the CRM system showing falling satisfaction or late payments. I would set a retention target, track it monthly, and check after six months whether the changes are working.
markingPoints: Gathers data on lost clients from records
Asks lost clients and front-line staff why they left
Looks for patterns by price, place, service or staff
Recommends specific improvements linked to the likely causes
Sets a retention target and monitors the effect of changes

essays.stem: Compare a transactional approach with a relationship approach to managing business customers, and recommend which a Kingston IT services firm should use for its larger clients.
essays.modelAnswer: In a transactional approach, each sale stands alone. The firm focuses on price, quick orders and winning the next deal, and there is little contact between sales. It is cheap to run and suits small, simple and one-off purchases. In a relationship approach, the firm builds long-term ties with the customer. It learns the client's business, plans with it, links staff at several levels, holds regular reviews and solves problems together. It costs more in time and staff, but brings repeat business, more trust, better information about needs and less pressure on price. For an IT services firm, larger clients buy complex, ongoing services such as network support and security, where trust, knowledge of the client's systems and quick response matter more than the lowest price. Losing such a client is costly, and new ones are hard to win. I would therefore recommend a relationship approach for larger clients, with account plans, service level agreements and regular reviews, while using a simpler transactional approach for small one-off jobs to keep costs down.
markingPoints: Describes the transactional approach and when it suits
Describes the relationship approach and its features
Compares costs and benefits of the two
Links the recommendation to the nature of IT services and larger clients
Recommends a relationship approach for large clients, with a simpler approach for small jobs

practical1.title: Prepare a key account plan for a major business customer
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack about a made-up Jamaican supplier and one of its largest business customers (for example a Kingston uniform maker that supplies a chain of private schools). The pack includes two years of sales, the cost to serve the account, a note of recent complaints and a list of the customer's staff. As a group, prepare a key account plan for the coming year. Give each member a named role: account lead (writes the customer profile and the plan's objectives, and chairs the group), relationship mapper (draws a chart of the customer's decision-making unit and shows which of your staff will link with each person), analyst (works out the account's sales trend and profit after the cost to serve in a spreadsheet, checking every figure twice), service planner (writes the service standards and the contact and review timetable), and risk and growth planner (lists risks to the account and opportunities to grow it, with actions). In a group of four, the account lead also writes the service standards. Put the plan together in one document of no more than four pages and present it to the assessor in 10 minutes. Every member speaks during the presentation.
materials: Computers with spreadsheet and word processor software
Account plan outline from the assessor (optional)
photos: The decision-making unit chart with links to your own staff
The spreadsheet showing the sales trend and account profit on screen
The service standards and contact and review timetable
The risk and growth table with actions and owners
The finished account plan and the group presenting it
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the plan
Customer profile and objectives are clear, specific and linked to the case facts
Decision-making unit is mapped correctly, with a named contact for each person
Account profit after the cost to serve is calculated correctly and checked twice
Service standards and review timetable are realistic and measurable
Risks and growth opportunities have sensible actions, owners and dates
Spoke clearly during the presentation and answered the assessor's questions
safety: Use only the made-up case data; do not bring in real customers' names or details
Keep printed drafts with the group and hand all copies to the assessor at the end
Treat group members with respect; challenge ideas, not people
Share the workload fairly and take a short break during the task

practical2.title: Role-play a quarterly review with a dissatisfied business customer
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a case: a made-up Jamaican firm whose key business customer (for example a resort group in Negril buying laundry services) is unhappy after late deliveries and a billing error, and is talking to a rival. As a group, prepare for, hold and follow up a quarterly account review meeting. Give each member a named role: account manager (leads the meeting for the supplier), operations manager (explains the causes of the problems and the fixes), customer's procurement manager (plays the client, using the assessor's role card), note-taker (records the discussion and the agreed actions), and observer (scores the meeting against a checklist and gives feedback). In a group of four, the note-taker also observes. Before the meeting, the supplier side prepares a one-page agenda and a short performance summary using the figures in the case. The meeting lasts 20 minutes. Afterwards the group writes a follow-up letter or email to the customer confirming the agreed actions, and an action log with owners and dates. Members then swap roles for a second, 10-minute run of the opening of the meeting so that each person practises a supplier role.
materials: Case brief and customer role card from the assessor
Computers with word processor and spreadsheet software
Agenda, action log and observer checklist templates
A table and chairs set up as a meeting room
photos: The agenda and performance summary prepared before the meeting
The meeting in progress, showing the work area and notes (faces only if all agree)
The note-taker's record of the discussion
The follow-up letter or email and the action log
checklist: Took a named role and prepared for it using the case facts
Supplier side listened, acknowledged the problems and did not blame others
Explained causes and fixes clearly, with realistic dates
Kept to the agenda and agreed specific actions with owners and dates
Follow-up letter or email is professional, accurate and matches the notes
Gave or received observer feedback calmly and suggested one improvement
Practised a supplier role in the second run
safety: Use only made-up names and case details; keep the notes confidential to the group and assessor
Stay calm and respectful in the role play; stop if anyone feels uncomfortable
Photograph faces only if every person agrees and the Centre allows it
Take a short break between the two runs
